title: Epiglottitis in Children
subject: Paediatrics
summary: Acute inflammation of the epiglottis can rapidly obstruct the airway. Prompt recognition, airway protection and targeted antibiotics are essential, especially where resources are limited.

sections.p: Epiglottitis is a bacterial infection causing swelling of the epiglottis and supraglottic structures, leading to potential airway obstruction.
b: Diagnosis is clinical; confirm with imaging or endoscopy only if airway is secure.
Key signs: drooling, dysphagia, muffled voice, tripod position, and stridor only on exertion.

sections.p: Severity is judged by airway compromise and systemic toxicity.
b: Mild: No stridor at rest, normal oxygen saturation, able to speak in short phrases.
Moderate: Stridor at rest, tachypnea, oxygen saturation 90‑94%, agitation.
Severe: Impending airway obstruction, severe distress, oxygen saturation <90%, cyanosis.

sections.p: In low‑resource settings the aetiology may differ from high‑income countries where Hib vaccination is routine.
b: Haemophilus influenzae type b – still common where Hib vaccine coverage is low.
Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, and Streptococcus pyogenes – opportunistic pathogens.
Viral co‑infection (e.g., influenza) can predispose to bacterial superinfection.
Local risk factors: recent upper‑respiratory infection, poor oral hygiene, traditional herbal preparations.

sections.p: The child often appears very ill but may not be febrile. The classic picture is a “tripod” posture with drooling and a muffled “hot potato” voice.
b: Rapid onset (hours) of dysphagia and drooling.
High‑pitched inspiratory stridor that worsens when supine.
Fever may be absent in early disease or in immunocompromised children.

t.b: Is the child maintaining adequate oxygenation? – <90% signals severe airway compromise; give supplemental O₂ and prepare airway.
Does the epiglottis appear enlarged (thumb sign)? – Positive supports diagnosis; negative does not exclude it.
Is there leukocytosis? – Elevated WBC supports bacterial infection but normal count does not rule it out.
Which organism is causing infection? – Positive culture guides definitive therapy; start empiric antibiotics before result.

sections.p: Airway obstruction can develop within minutes; delay is fatal.
b: Rapidly worsening stridor or inability to speak.
Drooling with inability to swallow secretions.
Hypoxia, bradycardia, or altered mental status.
Secondary pneumonia or sepsis.

sections.p: Secure the airway first, then treat the infection.
b: Call for senior help and arrange immediate airway protection – awake fiber‑optic intubation or emergency tracheostomy if intubation fails.
Give high‑flow oxygen and keep the child in a sitting position.
Empiric IV ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime) – covers Hib and most gram‑positive organisms; avoid oral antibiotics until airway is safe.
Add vancomycin if MRSA prevalence is high or if the child is severely ill and local resistance data suggest it.
Adjunctive steroids are not routinely recommended; they may be considered in severe airway edema where resources allow.
Monitor vitals, urine output, and mental status every 15‑30 minutes in the first hour.

sections.p: After stabilization, complete a 7‑10 day IV antibiotic course and arrange oral step‑down if appropriate.
b: Vaccinate all eligible children with Hib conjugate vaccine.
Educate caregivers on early signs of airway obstruction.
Review oral hygiene and discourage use of unsterile herbal remedies.
Croup – viral, produces a “steeple sign” on X‑ray, barky cough, and stridor that improves with humidified air.
Bacterial tracheitis – presents after a viral prodrome, with purulent secretions and may require intubation but lacks the thumb sign.
Retropharyngeal abscess – neck stiffness, limited neck extension, and a bulge posterior to the pharynx on lateral X‑ray.

sections.p: Reliance on a single test may give false reassurance.
b: Normal lateral neck X‑ray does not exclude early epiglottitis; clinical judgment overrides imaging.
Absence of fever does not rule out severe infection, especially in malnourished or HIV‑positive children.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden inability to speak or swallow
Stridor at rest or worsening despite oxygen
Cyanosis, bradycardia, or loss of consciousness

faq.q: Why is manipulation of the mouth dangerous in suspected epiglottitis?
faq.a: Touching the inflamed epiglottis can trigger reflex laryngospasm or vagal stimulation, causing sudden airway collapse.

faq.q: Can a child with epiglottitis be observed in a regular ward?
faq.a: Only after the airway is secured and the child is stable; otherwise they need a monitored setting with immediate surgical backup.

faq.q: Is the Hib vaccine no longer needed once a child has had epiglottitis?
faq.a: Vaccination is still recommended because natural infection does not guarantee lasting immunity and protects against future exposure.

exam: What immediate steps do you take when a child presents with drooling, muffled voice and stridor? — Assess airway, call senior, give high‑flow O₂, prepare for awake intubation or tracheostomy before any oral exam.
How does the thumb sign on a lateral neck X‑ray help you, and why might it be absent? — It shows a swollen epiglottis; early disease or poor positioning can hide it, so clinical signs trump imaging.
Why is ceftriaxone preferred as first‑line therapy in low‑resource settings? — It covers Hib and most common gram‑positive organisms with once‑daily dosing, and it is widely available.
When would you add vancomycin to the regimen? — If local MRSA rates are high, the child is severely ill, or cultures grow resistant gram‑positive organisms.

Differentiate epiglottitis from croup on examination and imaging. — Epiglottitis: drooling, tripod position, muffled voice, thumb sign; Croup: barky cough, inspiratory stridor that improves with humidity, steeple sign.
What are the red‑flag signs that indicate imminent airway failure? — Stridor at rest, inability to swallow secretions, hypoxia <90%, cyanosis, altered mental status.
Explain why oral examination is contraindicated until the airway is secured. — Direct contact can provoke laryngospasm and rapid obstruction, endangering the patient.

Outline the vaccination strategy to prevent epiglottitis in a low‑resource region. — Implement Hib conjugate vaccine at 6, 10, 14 weeks and a booster at 12‑15 months; integrate into existing immunisation programs.
